input:
We are required to calculate the factor by which the rate constant of a catalyst ageing test increases when the temperature is raised from 300 K to 340 K. The activation energy $E_a$ has a value of 113 kJ mol-1. It is assumed that the pre-exponential factor $A$ remains constant over the interval; the factor is conditional on this assumption holding, and the condition is stated because ageing changes the catalyst while the temperature changes, which is precisely the ground on which $A$ might not hold.

The Arrhenius relation expresses the rate constant $k$ at absolute temperature $T$ as:

$$k = A \exp\left(-\frac{E_a}{R T}\right)$$

where $k$ represents the rate constant, $A$ represents the pre-exponential factor, $E_a$ represents the activation energy, $R$ represents the gas constant, and $T$ represents the absolute temperature. If the ratio of the relation is formed at the two temperatures, $A$ is eliminated, so the ratio of the rate constants depends on the activation energy and the two temperatures alone. Over the interval of 40 K, the ratio is found to be 206.44, which means that the rate constant at the higher temperature is larger by that factor.

The size of the factor is the essential content of the result. An activation energy of this magnitude makes the exponential term very steep in temperature, and an ageing test run at the higher temperature compresses the exposure required at the lower temperature into a much shorter time, subject to the condition stated. Where the ageing mechanism itself is changed by the temperature, the compression does not represent a like-for-like acceleration, and the factor will overstate what the test proves; the result should therefore be understood as a rate ratio, and not as a lifetime ratio.

The pre-exponential factor $A$ is held constant over the interval; the factor is conditional on that holding, and the condition is stated here because ageing changes the catalyst while the temperature changes, which is the ground on which $A$ might not hold.

$$k = A \exp\left(-\frac{E_a}{R T}\right)$$

where $k$ denotes the rate constant, $A$ the pre-exponential factor, $E_a$ the activation energy, $R$ the gas constant, and $T$ the absolute temperature. Forming the ratio of the relation at the two temperatures eliminates $A$: the ratio of the rate constants depends on the activation energy and on the two temperatures alone. Over the 40 K interval the ratio is 206.44. The rate constant at the higher temperature is larger by that factor.

The size of the factor is the content of the result. An activation energy of this size makes the exponential term steep in temperature, and an ageing test run at the higher temperature compresses the exposure that the lower temperature would need into a much shorter time — on the stated condition.
